newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia PM urges no let-up in race to development.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia PM urges no let-up in race to development.

text.p: Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad warned Malaysians on Tuesday not to be complacent about the nation's fast-paced economy, saying the country must remain competitive if it is to achieve developed status by 2020.
Speaking at a national congress on making Malaysia an industrialised country in 23 years, Mahathir said high growth must be maintained while keeping inflation capped.
"We must grow at seven percent per annum for 30 years between 1990 and 2020," he told 800 government, corporate and community leaders at the Vision 2020 congress.
He said since growth slowed when economies matured, the nation should aim high in the early years "so that the average of seven percent would still be maintained".
Prices of essential goods must remain controlled, while wages should match productivity, he said.
"This is our strategy and the whole nation, from workers to top executives and the so-called tycoons, must understand the national strategy," Mahathir said.
Malaysia's economic expansion is now in its tenth year of more than eight percent growth with inflation maintained at an average of below four percent.
Mahathir, however, worries that complacency and overspending would ultimately derail his Vision 2020, a plan he launched in 1990 to turn the once agricultural-based economy into an industrial power.
"We do not want to have a fling, only to pay for it with prolonged poverty," he said.

In the race to boost development, Malaysia has embarked on a series of high-profile mega-projects, including the $5.5 billion Bakun hydro-electric dam and an ambitious Multimedia Super Corridor project providing a high-technology, high-speed communications zone for advanced computer applications.

It is also building a nine-billion-ringgit ($3.6-billion) new international airport and a futuristic administrative capital as part of the nine-by-30 mile (15-by-50 km) corridor extending south of Kuala Lumpur.

But the government has had to moderate growth after a scorching 9.5 percent expansion in its economy in 1995 raised concerns among foreign investors that the huge projects would overstrain the economy and add to its current account deficit problems.
Mahathir also said the government had to ultimately end its practice of protecting local businesses by keeping away foreign competition.
"We have to stop protecting our market. We have to open up in order to gain reciprocal access," he said.
